transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-10-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Owen Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Zenora CTO), Ravi Singh (Zenora Backend Lead), Marco Ibarra (Zenora SRE), Aisha Khan (Zenora PM)

Summary: quick probe into whether Zenora should go Hosted, Dedicated, or Private. Key drivers: p95 latency targets for snippet responses, streaming token throughput for real-time UI, concurrency during peak trading hours, and security/compliance gating for data residency. Agreed to run a 24-hour baseline and follow up with pricing + private deployment feasibility.

Topics: p95 SLOs, token/sec benchmarks, cold start behavior, autoscaling/burst capacity, KV cache/prefix caching, quantization tradeoffs, canary rollouts and fallbacks, SSO/KMS requirements.

Action items: see metadata list above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um today we wanted to, to understand your p95 goals and your token throughput so we can recommend hosted vs dedicated vs private. who wants to kick off?
[00:16] Lena: yeah hi thanks Maya. i'll give a quick background — Zenora runs a conversation agent in our product that augments live data dashboards. typical responses are 60-150 tokens but sometimes we have longer explainers, 400+ tokens. our main requirement is p95 under 300ms for the short snippets and p95 under 800ms for those longer responses, ideally.
[00:40] Ravi: and during market open we see spikes — concurrency hits 120 concurrent users hitting the inference endpoint with streaming enabled, about 20% of requests are streaming. peak token/sec aggregate we're guessing around 35k tokens/sec but that's a rough number.
[00:56] Owen: okay that's super helpful. when you say p95 300ms for short replies, is that end-to-end including network RTT or just inference time inside the model host?
[01:10] Lena: good call — sorry i mean end-to-end from our UI perspective, so includes network. we're in AWS us-east primarily, so latency budget for inference itself is about 180ms.
[01:22] Jordan: got it. so roughly 180ms inside the host for small contexts. any constraint on cost or preference for on-prem?
[01:32] Aisha: cost matters; we want to keep TCO reasonable. security is heavier though — some customers require data residency in eu-west for a subset of users. so private deployment for eu region or VPC options likely.
[01:44] Maya: ok, so three axes: latency budget, throughput concurrency, and compliance. quick shading: Hosted is fastest to onboard, Redwood Dedicated gives predictable capacity and lower per-token unit cost at scale, and Private gives you the residency and control but we need to evaluate network topology.
[02:02] Ravi: can we get an idea of the token/sec per-GPU ballpark for your verified models? we have a mix of smaller 3B style and a tuned 65B for summarization.
[02:14] Owen: sure — to give rough numbers: for a 3B-ish family on an A100-ish class we often see 400-800 tokens/sec depending on sequence length and batching; for 65B with quantization we quote more like 25-80 tokens/sec depending on quantization and kernel support. those are per-GPU numbers under continuous streaming optimized runtime.
[02:39] Marco: and how much does KV cache help? our prompts often repeat a lot of prefixes.
[02:45] Jordan: big impact — prefix/KV cache can reduce compute by 40-70% for repeated contexts. but the savings depend on how much you can reuse and how many unique session states you keep in memory. the downside is memory pressure per host.
[02:57] [crosstalk] Lena: right — our SRE is concerned about memory blowups if we retain per-session KV for many concurrent users.
[03:04] Owen: totally valid. we typically size Dedicated hosts with KV eviction tiers and set TTLs so hot sessions remain cached but stale ones flush. for Private we can tune memory allocations more aggressively if you control the infra.
[03:18] Maya: let's talk SLOs and fallback policies. if a 65B inference breaches p95 budget do you want automatic fallback to a smaller model or region failover?
[03:28] Ravi: fallback to a smaller model is preferable for UX continuity, as long as we can detect quality regressions.
[03:34] Jordan: we have tooling to run canary rollouts and A/B tests plus a quality gate to detect regressions on your guardrail prompts. we can wire your eval set so fallback is only used when quality drop is under a threshold you accept.
[03:48] Lena: on security — we need SSO + SAML for admin console, and KMS integration for keys. also audit logs retention 1 year. is that supported?
[03:58] Maya: yes, SAML SSO supported, RBAC in Console, KMS/HSM integration for private deployment and Dedicated optional. audit logs can be exported to your SIEM, retention is configurable with an add-on. we'll share the security pack.
[04:12] Aisha: how about cold starts and model load times? our UX can't tolerate long stalls when a rare long-form summarization request hits.
[04:21] Owen: this depends on how you set pool sizing and pre-warm policies. Dedicated gives you pinned model instances, so cold starts are basically eliminated. Hosted can keep warm pools for you but cost goes up. Private — you control preloads and may keep a local cache to avoid loading.
[04:36] Ravi: is there autoscaling granularity we should be aware of? we have very spiky load.
[04:42] Jordan: autoscaling in Dedicated works on reserved pools + burst capacity. we support fast scaling for stateless small-model routes; bigger models take longer to spin up so we recommend a hybrid: reserved capacity for large models and burst for smaller ones.
[04:56] [pause]
[05:05] Lena: ok let's dive into benchmarks — if we ran your harness what should we expect to provide?
[05:09] Owen: best is a representative prompt set plus distribution: percent short (0-80 tokens), mid (80-300), long (>300). also share expected concurrency curves: baseline, peak 5-minute, peak 1-minute. tokenization specifics (Byte-Pair / GPT-like) also help.
[05:26] Marco: for internal validation we also need headroom numbers. if we see 35k aggregate tokens/sec, what's safe to recommend for Dedicated sizing?
[05:34] Jordan: a rule-of-thumb we use: size for 1.4x expected peak to allow burst and headroom. so for 35k tokens/sec peak, we'd aim Dedicated capacity that supports ~50k tokens/sec aggregate, distributed across model classes.
[05:48] Ravi: and cost estimate?
[05:50] Maya: we'll prepare pricing — Dedicated is commit-based monthly, Hosted is pay-as-you-go. we'll send a few scenarios: conservative, balanced, aggressive.
[05:58] Aisha: one more — streaming tokens/sec per connection for user experience target is about 20-30 tokens/sec sustained when streaming. can your runtime do close to that per-connection?
[06:09] Owen: yes, per-connection streaming depends on model size; smaller models hit 30-60 tokens/sec easily, larger quantized ones settle at lower rates. network and client parsing also add overhead.
[06:20] Lena: we also run an offline summarizer that can be batched (not streaming) — so we might want different routes: low-latency streaming route and high-throughput batch route.
[06:30] Jordan: absolutely — we typically recommend separate routes with different autoscale policies and quantization profiles. batch routes can use heavier quantization to reduce cost.
[06:42] Ravi: any concerns about output determinism when you quantize? we need consistent quality for auditability.
[06:48] Owen: quantization can change distribution slightly. we can run gated evals — Redwood Optimize suggests quant profiles per workload and flags regressions. you can pin a model/quantization for production after validating.
[06:59] [15s pause, typing]
[07:20] Marco: network topology note: our EU customers must not store data outside EU. so private or VPC-hosted control plane is required for those segments.
[07:28] Maya: ok we'll show Private options where control plane is customer-managed and can be hosted in eu-west. Dedicated can also be region-bound with VPC peering.
[07:38] Lena: about observability — what metrics do we get? token-level cost, per-route p95, KV cache hit rates?
[07:45] Jordan: yes we expose token counts, cost/latency per-token, per-route histograms, tracing hooks for request lifecycle, KV hit ratios, and model-specific traces.
[07:56] Ravi: good. for our procurement team — we need an enterprise SLA with 99.9% uptime and incident response. is that part of Dedicated?
[08:04] Maya: Dedicated supports SLA tiers; we'll include SLA language in the follow-up. Private has different support matrix.
[08:11] Aisha: curious about fallbacks — region failover vs model fallback — any latency penalty on failover?
[08:18] Owen: region failover will add network latency and could violate your p95 target; model fallback within same region is usually preferable for latency-sensitive use. we can design fallback rules: try local smaller model first, then region failover if capacity saturates.
[08:35] Lena: can Redwood run a simulated peak test to show p95 under stress? we want actual numbers not just estimates.
[08:42] Jordan: yes, we can run a Redwood-led benchmark using your prompts and simulating concurrency. that'll produce p95 latency, tokens/sec, and tail behavior. we'll coordinate with Marco to run a 24-hour window.
[08:55] Ravi: ok great. what about tooling to monitor quality drift? our prompts change weekly.
[09:01] Owen: our Optimize product hooks eval sets into monitoring and can issue regression alerts when model outputs degrade versus a baseline. it can also recommend model/quantization switches.
[09:12] Maya: quick note on pricing sensitivity: Rugged cost control levers are batching, caching, and quantization. we can show expected unit cost delta when applying these to your workload.
[09:23] [crosstalk]
[09:28] Lena: curious if you have any real-world examples — customers who did Dedicated sizing for similar 35k token/sec peaks?
[09:34] Maya: yes — we recently worked with a fintech customer that had similar peaks — Dedicated with 12 GPUs across multiple zones plus a small warm pool in Hosted for burst gave consistent p95s without >30% extra cost.
[09:48] Ravi: any recommendation for per-connection streaming buffer sizes? we see client parse lag when packets are too choppy.
[09:55] Jordan: use moderate chunking (e.g., 64 token chunks) and set congestion window to avoid too many tiny packets. also keep-alive and http/2 or websockets for streaming is best.
[10:08] Marco: ok scheduling — we're aiming to pick a path by end of month. we'd like to run the benchmark next week.
[10:14] Maya: perfect — we'll run the baseline, share security docs, and pricing.
[10:19] Aisha: also please include a clear migration path if we start Hosted and move to Dedicated or Private later.
[10:25] Owen: we built the API and rollout tooling so models and routes can be migrated with minimal code changes — same SDKs, same routes, you just flip configs.
[10:35] Lena: any blockers on us running the initial test?
[10:38] Jordan: just the prompt set and permission to hit the endpoints. for private deployment feasibility we need to review your network diagrams.
[10:46] [long pause, minor chatter about calendars]
[11:10] Maya: recap — 1) Redwood runs a 24-hour benchmark using your prompt set and simulated concurrency; 2) Redwood shares pricing scenarios and security pack; 3) schedule private-feasibility deep-dive next week; 4) Marco to confirm data residency constraints.
[11:28] Lena: yep that's it. thanks all.
[11:31] Maya: thank you, we'll follow up with calendar invites and docs.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional speaker label swaps (some segments labeled Jordan when Owen speaks), some proper nouns slightly garbled (e.g., K-V cash for KV cache), but all technical points captured.
